name: Meerut
region: North of Delhi — a major Company garrison
tagline: Where troopers refused the cartridge and the uprising began.
description: Meerut was one of the largest British Indian military stations, home to regiments of the Bengal Army. The public punishment of 85 troopers of the 3rd Bengal Light Cavalry on 9 May 1857 set the cantonment ablaze with anger; the next evening, sepoys rose, freed the prisoners and marched on Delhi.
timelineNote: Documents record the court-martial of the 85 troopers (May 1857) and the mutiny of Sunday 10 May 1857.

name: Delhi
region: The Mughal capital on the Yamuna
tagline: The symbolic heart of the rebellion — the Red Fort and the last Mughal emperor.
description: Delhi was the seat of the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar, though by 1857 his authority had shrunk to the Red Fort. When the Meerut sepoys arrived on 11 May and the city's regiments joined them, Delhi became the rebellion's political centre — holding the capital until British columns stormed it in September 1857.
timelineNote: From 11 May to 20 September 1857, Delhi was held by the sepoys and their supporters.

name: Kanpur
region: A trading and garrison town on the Ganga
tagline: Site of the siege and the most contested episodes of the war.
description: Kanpur (Cawnpore to the British) held a British garrison and a large Indian population. In June 1857 the garrison was besieged by forces under Nana Sahib, surrendered on promise of safe passage, and was cut down at the river landing at Satichaura Ghat. The later massacre of prisoners at the Bibighar made Kanpur infamous in Europe and hardened the war.
timelineNote: Siege and surrender, June 1857; the town was retaken by the British in the same month.

name: Lucknow
tagline: The capital of annexed Awadh — where the siege burned longest.
description: Awadh, one of the richest regions of India, was annexed by the East India Company in 1856, dispossessing its taluqdars and court. When the rebellion broke, Lucknow's sepoys and city rose against Company rule. The Residency was besieged from June 1857; relief columns fought through in September and November, and the city fell to a full assault in March 1858.
timelineNote: Residency besieged June 1857; city recaptured March 1858.

name: Jhansi
tagline: The state annexed by the doctrine of lapse — defended by Lakshmibai.
description: Jhansi was a small princely state in Bundelkhand. After its ruler died without a male heir in 1853, the Company annexed Jhansi under the doctrine of lapse, refusing to recognise her adoption. When Jhansi's garrison rebelled in 1857, the Rani Lakshmibai emerged as the leader of its defence. British forces stormed the fort in April 1858; Lakshmibai escaped and was killed in battle near Gwalior in June 1858.

name: Shivneri
region: Hill fort above Junnar, Pune district
tagline: Birthplace of Swarajya — by tradition the fort where Shivaji was born.
description: Shivneri is a hill fort commanding the town of Junnar in the northern Ghats. By tradition, Shivaji was born here in February 1630 to Jijabai and Shahaji Bhonsle. The fort's architecture — gates, bastions and water tanks — belongs to the period of the Deccan sultanates and the early Maratha rise.
timelineNote: Traditionally the birthplace of Shivaji (1630); the date rests on the chronicles.

name: Pune
region: Deccan plateau town and jagir estate
tagline: The jagir around which the young Shivaji began to gather the hill country.
description: Pune and its surrounding villages formed the estate (jagir) granted to the Bhonsles in the 1630s–40s, administered during Shivaji's boyhood under guardians like Dadoji Konddeo. From this base, the young prince drew the mavals of the neighbouring valleys into the project of Swarajya.

name: Torna Fort
region: Hill fort west of Pune (Velhe range)
tagline: Prachandgad — the first great fort taken for Swarajya.
description: Torna, one of the largest forts of its kind in the Sahyadri, was taken by Shivaji around 1646 and renamed Prachandgad. The treasure found within reportedly helped fund the movement's early expansion.

name: Rajgad
region: Hill fort in the Sahyadri, Pune district
tagline: The mountain capital where the new power was built.
description: Rajgad (formerly Murumbdev) was developed from about 1648–49 as Shivaji's principal seat. Its wide plateau demanded immense building works — reservoirs, gates, dwellings and workshops — and it served as the centre of the expanding state for over two decades.
timelineNote: Capital stronghold c. 1648–49 onward; later superseded by Raigad.

name: Kondhana / Sinhagad
tagline: The fortress of the Singh (lion) — consolidated in the years of expansion.
description: Kondhana, later celebrated as Sinhagad, was among the forts captured and consolidated in the late 1640s–1650s. Its fall was later famously linked by tradition to the death of Tanaji Malusare in a night assault (1670), a story of the recovery campaigns.
timelineNote: Captured in the 1640s–50s; the 1670 night assault is remembered in tradition.

name: Pratapgad
region: Hill fort in the Mahabaleshwar range, Satara district
tagline: The fort of doom — where Afzal Khan fell (10 November 1659).
description: Pratapgad was built as an advanced stronghold on the Konkan route south of the Sahyadri. Below its walls, on 10 November 1659, the confrontation between Shivaji and the Bijapur general Afzal Khan ended with the general's death and the rout of his army — the decisive victory of the early Swarajya.
timelineNote: Site of the 10 November 1659 meeting and battle.

name: Panhala
tagline: The place of the great monsoon siege and the night escape.
description: Panhala, one of the largest forts of the region, was held by Shivaji in 1660 when Siddi Jauhar's Bijapur army besieged it through the monsoon. In July 1660 Shivaji escaped by night through the ghats toward Vishalgad, while a rearguard held the pass at Ghod Khind.

name: Vishalgad
region: Hill fort in the Kolhapur ghats
tagline: The refuge reached after the escape from Panhala.
description: Vishalgad was the destination of Shivaji's night escape from Panhala. Between the two forts lay the defile of Ghod Khind (Pavankhind), where Baji Prabhu Deshpande's rearguard gave their lives holding the pass. (Coordinates are approximate for the broad fort region.)
timelineNote: Reached during the escape of July 1660.

name: Surat
region: Mughal port of western India (today in Gujarat)
tagline: The emporium of the Indian Ocean — struck in January 1664.
description: Surat was the greatest commercial port of Mughal western India, home to traders and factories from across the Indian Ocean and Europe, including the English East India Company. In January 1664 Shivaji's raid took the town and its wealth, an act recorded in European letters and Persian chronicles alike.
timelineNote: Raided January 1664; a second raid occurred in 1670.

name: Agra
region: Mughal imperial capital (today in Uttar Pradesh)
tagline: The court where Swarajya's leader was received — and from which he escaped.
description: Agra, the Mughal capital of Aurangzeb, was where Shivaji was detained after his reception at court in May 1666, following the Treaty of Purandar. The escape that followed — recounted in chronicles and European records — saw him journey across the subcontinent and return to the Konkan by months' end.

name: Raigad
region: Hill fort in the Konkan ghats, Raigad district
tagline: The capital and coronation seat of the Chhatrapati.
description: Raigad was developed after the mid-1660s as the movement's lasting capital. On 6 June 1674 Shivaji was crowned here with full sovereign ceremonies, proclaiming the Maratha country an independent state — Chhatrapati. The fort's ruins, gates and the site of the coronation remain its most celebrated features.
timelineNote: Capital from the late 1660s; coronation 6 June 1674.
